passage:
Paragraph A
A planet in orbit around another star is, from the Earth, an object of almost no brightness sitting immediately beside an object of overwhelming brightness. Seeing it directly is roughly the problem of picking out a moth beside a searchlight. For most of the twentieth century this was reason enough to assume that planets outside our own system, if they existed at all, would never be catalogued. They are now counted in the thousands, and almost none of them have been seen.

Paragraph B
The method that found the first of them measures the star rather than the planet. A planet does not simply orbit its star; the two bodies orbit their common centre of mass, so the star itself traces a small circle. As it moves slightly towards us and then slightly away, the wavelengths of its light are alternately squeezed and stretched, and that shift can be measured with a sufficiently good spectrograph. In 1995 this technique revealed 51 Pegasi b, a hot gas giant hugging its star at about half the size of Jupiter, whose wobble was unmistakable.

Paragraph C
The reason that first discovery was a large planet in a tight orbit is not an accident of luck but a property of the method. A massive planet tugs its star harder, and a close planet completes its circuit quickly, so the signal is both stronger and repeats sooner. The technique is therefore biased: it finds the heavy and the near first, and it took years of patient observation before smaller, slower worlds began to emerge from the same data.

Paragraph D
The second great method also ignores the planet itself and watches the starlight. If the orbit happens to cross our line of sight, the planet passes in front of its star once each circuit and blocks a small fraction of the light. Recording the brightness over time produces a light curve, and a repeating dip of the same depth and duration is the signature of a transit. From the interval between dips and an estimate of the star's mass, the size of the orbit can be calculated; from the depth of the dip, the size of the planet.

Paragraph E
This method carries a bias of its own, and it is a severe one. The alignment has to be nearly edge-on, and for most planetary systems it is not, so the great majority of planets can never transit as seen from here. What redeems the technique is that a single telescope can watch many thousands of stars at once and let statistics do the work. That is what NASA's Kepler mission did, and the conclusion drawn from its haul was not about any individual world but about all of them: small planets turned out to be very common, and there are more planets in our galaxy than there are stars.

Paragraph F
A third approach exploits an effect first described by Einstein — gravity's ability to warp and bend starlight. When one star passes in front of another as seen from the Earth, the nearer star acts as a lens and briefly magnifies the more distant one. A planet orbiting the nearer star adds its own short spike to that brightening. Microlensing is uniquely able to find planets at large distances from their stars, but it has an unfortunate property: the alignment never repeats, so each detection is a single event that cannot be checked by looking again.

Paragraph G
Direct imaging, the obvious method, remains the hardest. The photons of the planet must be separated from a flood of starlight, and so far this has mainly been achieved for giant planets still so hot from their formation that they glow of their own accord. Two engineering answers are being pursued. A coronagraph is a system of masks, prisms and detectors that suppresses the starlight inside the telescope, aided by deformable mirrors carrying thousands of tiny actuators that flex in real time. A starshade would do the same job outside the telescope: a sunflower-shaped spacecraft the size of a baseball diamond, unfolding like origami and flying far ahead to cast a shadow.

Paragraph H
Once a planet is known, the same starlight can be made to describe it. During a transit a little of the star's light passes through the planet's atmosphere before continuing to us, and the gases there absorb particular wavelengths. Spreading that light out, as a prism splits white light into a spectrum, reveals which wavelengths are missing and therefore which molecules are present; helium and water vapour have both been identified this way. It is an indirect procedure resting on an indirect detection, which is a fair description of the whole field.

(Glossary: spectrograph: an instrument that spreads light into its component wavelengths and records them; light curve: a graph of an object's brightness over time; transit: the passage of a planet across the face of its star; actuator: a small device that moves or controls a mechanism.)
